answer:
HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded answer): The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants varies sharply and systematically with habitat type in Barcelona province. Measured as the gardening share of all non-native plant occurrences (Σn.gard/Σn.total per habitat — the definition the hypothesis rests on, and the only one whose ranking is fully robust to the zero-total-plot sensitivity check), gardening prevalence is highest in wetlands (55.8%, 29/52) and coastal habitats (53.5%, 23/43), and in forest habitats the few non-native plants that do occur are almost exclusively gardening escapes (broad-leaved forests 100% — 4/4; coniferous forests 87.5% — 7/8). It is intermediate in scrublands (40.0%), riparian zones (36.5%) and meadows (30.8%), and lowest in croplands (18.5%, where agriculture/forestry and accidental introductions dominate) and rock outcrops (0%, 0/1). Urban plots are the notable exception to a simple "disturbance = gardening" story: they host the largest absolute number of gardening species (45 of the 169 gardening records province-wide, and gardening species occur in ~48% of urban plots — the second-highest incidence), yet their gardening share is only ~29.8% because urban plots also accumulate many unintentionally introduced species. In short: gardening is the dominant introduction route in wet, coastal and forest habitats, whereas non-gardening pathways dominate in croplands, urban areas and rocky sites. Supportive context: Catalonia-wide, gardening's share of new introductions rose from 17% (before 1500) to 75% (1985–2019), so the wet/coastal pattern reflects the region-wide ascendance of ornamental introductions.

KEY EVIDENCE (ranked table, all 632 plots; see outputs/habitat_gardening_prevalence.csv):
- Occurrence share (Σn.gard/Σn.total): Broad-leaved forests 1.000, Coniferous forests 0.875, Wetlands 0.558, Coastal 0.535, Scrublands 0.400, Riparian 0.365, Meadows 0.308, Urban 0.298, Croplands 0.185, Rock outcrops 0.000.
- Mean per-plot share (plots with n.total>0) gives the same ordering at habitat level (e.g., Wetlands 0.647, Urban 0.287, Croplands 0.171).
- Incidence (fraction of all plots in the habitat with n.gard>0) gives a different emphasis: Wetlands 0.500 and Urban 0.477 lead, forests trail (0.04–0.07) — i.e., forests have high share but low occurrence, urban has high frequency but low share.
- Sensitivity (excluding 441 zero-total plots): occurrence-share ranking is IDENTICAL (10/10 positions, pairwise agreement 1.0); incidence ranking changes (urban drops from 2nd to 8th when denominators are invaded plots only), so incidence-based claims are stated separately and not used for the final hypothesis.
- Supportive test (clearly labeled secondary): chi-square on the pooled pathway × habitat table (10 habitats × gardening/non-gardening): X²=48.83, df=9, p≈1.8e-07 — habitat and pathway are strongly associated — with the caveat that several expected counts are <5 (min 0.35, driven by forest/scrub/rock cells with totals of 1–8).
- Temporal context: gardening share per period = 0.17 (pre-1500), 0.45 (1501–1900), 0.49 (1901–1984), 0.75 (1985–2019).
- n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo==n.total verified in all 632 rows before analysis; total 481 non-native occurrences, 169 via gardening.

WORKFLOW: (1) parsed the tab-separated invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots × 37 vars) and validated count consistency; (2) aggregated per habitat the three approved prevalence metrics; (3) reran all metrics excluding zero-total plots and compared rankings (occurrence-share ranking unchanged, incidence ranking materially different — reported, not silently resolved); (4) ran one minimal chi-square as supportive evidence; (5) extracted one sentence of temporal context from the contingency table; (6) phylogeny deliberately skipped per instruction (tip-label mismatches irrelevant here); historical land-use variables not used in the comparison, consistent with the approved plan.

LIMITATIONS/UNCERTAINTIES: (a) counts are species-per-plot, so "share of species richness" is implemented as the within-plot mean share; a true cross-plot distinct-species richness is not computable from these files (no species×habitat incidence table); (b) forest and scrubland shares rest on very few total occurrences (4, 8, and 5) — direction is robust but magnitude is imprecise; (c) the chi-square approximation is strained by sparse cells (permutation test would be more exact); (d) the dataset covers Barcelona province plots only, while the temporal context is Catalonia-wide.

payload.hypothesis: Gardening-introduced plants dominate the non-native flora of wetlands (~56%), coastal habitats (~54%) and forests (where the sparse non-native flora is 88–100% gardening-derived), are intermediate in scrublands, riparian zones and meadows (31–40%), and are least prevalent in croplands (~19%) and rock outcrops (0%); urban plots host the most gardening species in absolute terms and the second-highest per-plot frequency but only a ~30% share because unintentional introductions also accumulate there. This habitat gradient parallels the regional rise of gardening as an introduction pathway (17% of pre-1500 introductions vs 75% in 1985–2019).
payload.workflow: Parsed tab-separated invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots), validated pathway-count consistency, computed three prevalence metrics per habitat (pooled occurrence share, mean per-plot share, incidence), ran the zero-total-plot sensitivity check (occurrence-share ranking unchanged; incidence ranking shifted, both reported), one supportive chi-square on the pooled pathway×habitat table, and one sentence of temporal context from temporal_trends_contingency_table.csv; phylogeny excluded per instruction.
